1. Scientific Analysis

Across 243-313 K the 31P NMR of the mixed G2/TEP Mg-electrolyte shows the classic signature of chemical exchange in the competitive-solvation system: at low temperature multiple 31P environments (a sharp ~-6 ppm component with a co-located shoulder ~-5.6 ppm and a broad ~-3.5 ppm component) are resolved in the slow-exchange regime, and as temperature rises the lines broaden-then-coalesce into a single averaged resonance by 278 K, with the residual line continuing to narrow toward 313 K. The dominant FWHM trend is the most robust and physically interpretable metric, decreasing monotonically and steeply with T — consistent with faster exchange and motional narrowing at higher temperature. The resolved-component count captures the coalescence as a stepwise 3-to-1 transition between 258 and 278 K. The dominant-peak center is a poor trend metric here because it splices together non-equivalent assignments across the two regimes; the 'All resolved peak positions' panel is more honest, showing distinct low-T environments converging toward the high-T averaged position. Two features qualify the exchange narrative. First, the total integrated area halves at the same temperature as the component collapse; because ideal exchange conserves magnetization, this points to either a quantification/integration artifact introduced by the model-topology switch or a genuine acquisition/relaxation effect (e.g. T1 changes over T with fixed recycle delay) — it cannot be resolved from the present data and should not be interpreted as speciation change. Second, the low-T residuals are coherent rather than noise-level, and even a 3-component full-Voigt fit leaves a dispersive oscillation at the sharp peak's inner flank, indicating the slow-exchange lineshape is more structured than the locked model fully captures. All fits meet quality gates, and the qualitative coalescence conclusion is well supported; however, the Hz-domain linewidths and any T2* derived from them are unreliable because the wrong Larmor frequency (161.98 vs reported 202 MHz) was used, and must be recomputed before any relaxation interpretation.

5. Scientific Claims

Claim 1: The 31P NMR of the mixed G2/TEP Mg-electrolyte exhibits temperature-dependent chemical exchange: multiple resolved 31P environments in the slow-exchange regime at low temperature (3 components at 243-258 K) coalesce into a single motionally-averaged resonance by 278 K, accompanied by a monotonic, steep decrease in dominant-peak linewidth from ~3.4 ppm to ~0.19 ppm across 243-313 K.

Scientific Impact: Directly characterizes competitive solvation dynamics of Mg2+ between diglyme and triethyl phosphate, providing the exchange/coalescence temperature window that constrains solvation-shell exchange rates relevant to electrolyte design and ion-transport mechanisms.

Literature Search Query: Has anyone quantified the coalescence temperature and exchange rate of 31P solvation environments in mixed glyme/phosphate Mg-electrolytes to distinguish competitive solvation structures?

Keywords: 31P NMR, chemical exchange, coalescence, competitive solvation, Mg electrolyte, variable-temperature NMR

Claim 2: The total 31P integrated area drops by roughly half (~1.1e9 to ~0.5e9) coincident with the low-to-high-temperature component-count collapse, an effect not explained by exchange (which conserves magnetization) and consistent with either a quantification artifact from the model-topology switch or a temperature-dependent acquisition/relaxation effect.

Scientific Impact: Flags a potential quantitation pitfall in VT-NMR speciation of this system: if the area change is acquisition-driven (e.g. T1/recycle-delay), relative populations across the coalescence would be biased, affecting any solvation-population interpretation.

Literature Search Query: Has anyone verified magnetization conservation across the coalescence transition in VT 31P NMR of Mg-electrolytes, or is the apparent intensity change an artifact of model switching or incomplete relaxation recovery?

Keywords: integrated intensity, quantitative NMR, T1 relaxation, coalescence artifact, variable-temperature NMR

6. Caveats & Limitations

The component count is regime-prescribed rather than fully data-driven; per domain rules this can hide or manufacture discontinuities, so the 3-to-1 collapse should be regarded as data-consistent but not independently proven by count alone. The dominant-peak center 'trend' is largely an artifact of splicing non-equivalent assignments across the two regimes and should not be over-interpreted. The integrated-area drop is unexplained by exchange and may be a quantification artifact from the model switch or an acquisition/relaxation effect; magnetization conservation was not verified. Critically, the Larmor frequency used for Hz conversions (assumed 161.98 MHz for indices 2-4) contradicts the reported 202 MHz spectrometer frequency, so all Hz-domain linewidths and any T2* estimates are quantitatively unreliable and must be recomputed. Fit quality gates are met throughout, but low-T residuals remain coherent, indicating the slow-exchange lineshape is not fully captured. No adaptive refits or alternate-model comparisons were performed.
